newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb judge takes up closed TV admission.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb judge takes up closed TV admission.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing case Thursday took up the delicate issue of who among hundreds of victims should be admitted to a special closed telecast of the bombing trial to be shown in Oklahoma City.

U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch said at the second day of a pre-trial hearing that he was concerned about victims of the blast, which killed 168 people, having to line up before dawn to ensure a seat at the telecast.

Under a recently passed anti-terrorism act, victims of the bombing including the injured and relatives of the dead will be able to view the proceedings via closed circuit television in a yet-to-be determined location in Oklahoma City.

Timothy McVeigh and Terry Nichols are charged in the April 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in which about 500 people were injured in addition to the dead. The defendants will be tried separately. McVeigh will be tried first and his case is expected to begin sometime next year.

Because the case has been moved to Denver to ensure fairness, many victims have said it will be a hardship for them to attend the trials. There are more than 1,000 requests to attend the special telecast and Matsch must decide how to allot the seats.
Local media from Oklahoma City are also hoping to receive some of the seats at the telecast, but prosecutors objected, saying the victims need to watch the proceedings in privacy.
Matsch told prosecutors to file with the court next week their view of whether seating should be prioritized according to hardship and suffering.

Prosecutor Vickie Behenna said she was hesitant to suggest that certain people, such as those who lost businesses near the bombing site, be given different consideration than people who lost loved ones or were injured themselves.
Matsch said it was his duty to decide how to classify the victims but he wanted to know what the government's view was.
Several victims have attended all the pre-trial hearings. Paul Heath, a spokesman for the victims, said there would probably not be enough seats for all the people who wanted to watch the telecast.

Matsch also held a closed-door hearing Thursday on whether classified information that certain federal agencies may have should be released to the defendants. McVeigh's defence team has suggested that international terrorists may have been responsible for the bombing and wants any information that may exist on bomb threats or warnings from other countries.

Lead prosecutor Joseph Hartzler declined to comment on the progress of the closed-door hearing. But he told reporters scheduling issues, including possibly setting a trial date, would be discussed Friday, along with security measures to make sure the closed circuit trial telecast is not pirated.
